_comment: The machine-readable face of ROADMAP.md. Every item here is verified in that document as NOT built (G1 is the exception: it shipped, and is kept so the bot closes its issue instead of reopening it). Change a status here and the curator bot opens or closes the matching issue; nothing else in this repo opens roadmap issues by hand. N1-N3/X7 were added 2026-11-03 from docs/ROADMAP-PROPOSED.md: they repair the claim the product is sold on before any new surface is added. The cap was raised from 4 to 8 so this four-item cycle can be claimed in parallel; lower it again once they land. V1 and A1/E2-E9 were added the same day as a verified backlog: each records the command or reproduction that justified it, and three candidate items were dropped because probing disproved them (exit codes, the pip Dependabot config, demo accessibility).

items.title: feat(verifier): audit MCP010 patches so an absurd timeout is not accepted
items.summary: MCP010 was in AUTOFIXABLE with no entry in SMELLS or REMEDY_MARKERS, so the audit accepted any patch that cleared the rule - including `timeout=float('inf')`.
items.motivation: The product's whole claim is that the scanner can be fooled and the verifier cannot. MCP010 was the one rule where the verifier could be fooled, and it was fixable. Found by auditing the audit, which is why the fix ships with a structural guard rather than only a patch.
acceptance_criteria: timeout=None, float('inf'), 10**9, 1e9 and 86400 are rejected
timeout=10, 2.5 and TIMEOUT_SECONDS are accepted
test_every_fixable_rule_is_covered_by_the_audit fails if a rule joins AUTOFIXABLE unaudited

items.title: fix(agent): run the target's test suite against the target root — gate 3 never runs today
items.summary: `agent.py` copies only the target FILE into the temp workspace, so `run_tests()` finds no `test_*.py` and returns `None`. `cli.py` then renders that `None` as 'unchanged / passing'. A target whose own tests fail still comes out `verified=True`.
items.motivation: Gate 3 is one of the three checks the README sells: 'It still works - the target's own pytest suite must pass after the patch.' It cannot run: the workspace holds one file and no suite. A verification product whose gate silently does nothing is worth less than one that admits it has two gates. Reproduced offline: a target with a deliberately failing test suite produced `tests_ok=None` and `verified=True`, while `run_tests()` on the real project directory returned `False`.
acceptance_criteria: The workspace is materialised from the target's ROOT (excluding .git, venvs, __pycache__, node_modules), so the patched module is what the tests import
`run_tests` is called with the root, not `workspace.parent`
`tests_ok` is True / False / null plus a `tests_detail` string; both are exposed in `--json`
A null result is rendered as 'tests not run', never as 'passing', in human output
A target whose tests fail after the patch is not verified and `--apply` does not write
A `--tests-root PATH` override and a wall-clock cap exist so a monorepo cannot stall a dry run
The existing 76 tests still pass and `--no-tests` still skips the gate, visibly recorded

items.title: test(agent): pin all three gates with a gate matrix — the first test that runs check_tests=True
items.summary: All 12 tests in `tests/test_agent.py` pass `check_tests=False`, and grepping `tests/` for `tests_ok`, `run_tests` or `--no-tests` returns nothing. Gate 3 has zero coverage, which is why the defect in N1 survived review.
items.motivation: `ROADMAP.md` says every invariant 'is already pinned by a test'. Gate 3 is not. Without a matrix that exercises each gate independently, a refactor can delete a check and leave the suite green - the exact failure this repository is built to argue against.
acceptance_criteria: `tests/fixtures/project_with_failing_tests/` - a module plus a `test_*.py` that fails after the canonical patch; `project_with_passing_tests/` and `project_with_no_tests/` alongside it
`tests/test_gates.py` rejects a patch for each gate in turn: a patch that clears gates 1 and 2 but fails exactly one gate must not verify
A documentation invariant fails if the gate table in README.md disagrees with a `GATES` constant in the code
Mutation check recorded in the PR: commenting out the `run_tests` call makes `pytest` go red
The suite grows beyond 76 tests and needs no API key or network

items.title: fix(proof): reconcile the published numbers — runs.json reports zero tokens with a non-zero cost
items.summary: `docs/data/runs.json` reports `input_tokens: 0, output_tokens: 0` alongside `cost_usd: 0.0226` - a shape `clients.py:_record` cannot produce. Related drift: `README.md` quotes 46 tests where the suite collects 76.
items.motivation: This is the file behind the live demo page, and the product's claim is that every number on it is checkable. The cheapest number on the page contradicts itself, so a sceptic discounts the expensive ones. G7 and G9 describe this same defect from two angles and should merge into this item.
acceptance_criteria: The 2026-10-28 run is either re-captured with a key, or marked `"telemetry": "pre-token-capture"` with unsubstantiated token fields no longer rendered
A test asserts `input_tokens + output_tokens > 0 => cost_usd > 0`, that mock runs carry explicit nulls, and that the key set matches what `docs/index.html` reads
A test asserts the test count quoted in README.md equals `pytest --collect-only -q`
`roadmap.json` merges G7 and G9 into this item rather than tracking one defect twice
`docs/data/scan.json` is left alone - it already reproduces byte-for-byte

items.title: feat(agent): bound the test-gate execution - no network, read-only outside the workspace
items.summary: `verifier.py:run_tests` executes the target's test suite with the caller's privileges, network and working directory. Today that risk is latent only because the gate is broken (N1); making the gate work makes it live.
items.motivation: N1 turns on code execution against other people's repositories. The README already warns that the verifier may run the target's tests and that it should not be pointed at untrusted code outside a sandbox - a warning is not a boundary. This must be tracked before N1 lands so the repair does not quietly widen the blast radius.
acceptance_criteria: The test gate runs in a subprocess with no network by default and an explicit `--allow-network` opt-in
The target root is bound read-only; only the throwaway workspace copy is writable
A wall-clock cap is enforced and reported as a failed gate, not a pass
`--help` and the report header state the execution boundary in one line
A fixture whose test writes to `../` or opens a socket reports the gate as blocked rather than passing
Platforms without the primitive get a documented, visible fallback - not a silent downgrade

items.title: fix(verifier): audit_patch fails open when the patched line already exists elsewhere in the file
items.summary: `audit_patch()` builds its `added` set as lines of `after` that are not in `set(before.splitlines())` (`verifier.py:253-254`) and returns `[]` as soon as that set is empty (`:255`). If the patch's replacement line already appears somewhere else in the file, the patch is never audited at all.
items.motivation: Reproduced: flipping `subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True)` to `subprocess.run(cmd, shell=False, check=False)` - the exact anti-pattern `SMELLS['MCP005']` exists to reject - returned `[]` (accepted, no checks run) because an identical line already existed in the file. The module docstring says 'Rejection is fail-closed on purpose'; this path is fail-open. Duplicated boilerplate is the common case in real servers, so the audit is blind precisely where the code is repetitive. SECURITY.md lists verifier bypasses as a first-class report class, which makes this the most serious finding in the repository.
acceptance_criteria: A diff-based added-line computation (difflib opcodes on before/after, not set membership) so a rewritten line is always visible to the audit
A regression case proves the MCP005 anti-pattern is rejected even when an identical line exists elsewhere in the file
A matching good patch (canonical remedy, duplicate line present) is still accepted - no false rejection
A test asserts `audit_patch` never returns `[]` for a rule in AUTOFIXABLE when the targeted line actually changed

items.title: fix(cli): make --apply refuse to overwrite without a backup or a version-control check
items.summary: `--apply` writes the patch with a bare `target.write_text(...)` (`cli.py:86`). Outside a git repository there is no backup, no confirmation and no warning - the only warning that exists fires for paths whose parent directory happens to be named `examples`.
items.motivation: Reproduced: `--apply` on a copy of a fixture in `/tmp/nogit/` overwrote the file, exited 0, printed 'applied to ...' and created no backup. For a tool whose selling point is that it never writes without verification, the write path itself should say whether the previous contents are recoverable. The README instructs users to use a disposable clone, but nothing checks that they did.
acceptance_criteria: `--apply` warns visibly and requires an explicit acknowledgement flag when the target is not inside a git work tree
A `.bak` copy (or the original bytes in the report) is written before the target is modified
The report states where the previous contents can be recovered from
A test asserts the target is byte-identical after an interrupted or refused apply

items.title: fix(cli): report unknown model pricing instead of silently claiming the run cost $0.00
items.summary: `clients.py:61` prices a run with `MODEL_PRICES.get(model, (0.0, 0.0))`. Any model ID supplied through `AUTOFIX_MODEL_*` that is not in that table is priced at zero, so the run reports `~$0.0000`.
items.motivation: Reproduced: with `AUTOFIX_MODEL_PATCH=nvidia/some-new-model`, a million prompt and a million completion tokens cost `0.0`. The README and the demo page publish cost, and the whole positioning is that the numbers are checkable. A silent zero is worse than 'unknown' because it looks like a measurement. Token Factory's lineup changes - `--preflight` exists precisely because of that - so an unpriced model is the expected case, not an exotic one.
acceptance_criteria: An unpriced model yields `cost_usd: null` plus a `cost_note` naming the model, never `0.0`
The human report prints 'cost unknown (no price for <model>)' rather than a currency figure
A test covers a model ID absent from MODEL_PRICES
`--json` consumers can distinguish 'free' from 'not priced'

items.title: fix(cli): --json emits two different schemas - a clean run has no usage, triage or bucket keys
items.summary: A clean target returns `{before, clean, target}`; a target with findings returns fourteen keys including `usage`, `triage`, `fixed`, `refused`, `skipped`, `attempts`. Same flag, two documents.
items.motivation: Measured directly: `--json` on `examples/clean_server.py` emits three keys, on `examples/vulnerable_server.py` fourteen. Every consumer - the Action in G5, the proof artifact in G3, any CI parser - has to special-case the clean path. The early return is `agent.py:139-144`.
acceptance_criteria: Every `--json` document carries the same key set, with empty lists/zeroed usage for a clean run
A schema test asserts the key set is identical across all three fixtures
A `schema_version` field exists so the next change to this shape is not a silent break

items.title: fix(cli): a non-UTF-8 target crashes with a traceback instead of a clean error
items.summary: `agent.py` reads the target with `read_text(encoding="utf-8")`. A file containing Latin-1 bytes raises `UnicodeDecodeError` from the middle of the scanner stack, and the user sees a codec traceback.
items.motivation: Reproduced with a Latin-1 source file: `UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0xff`. Python source files predating PEP 263 defaults, vendored code with other encodings, and mixed-encoding repositories are common enough that the tool should say 'this file is not UTF-8, here is the byte offset' rather than dumping an internal stack trace.
acceptance_criteria: A non-decodable target produces one actionable error line naming the file and byte offset, with no traceback
Detection honours a PEP 263 coding cookie when present
A test covers a Latin-1 fixture and asserts no traceback in stderr

items.title: perf(agent): stop re-scanning the file twice per run - score_of() discards the diagnostics it just computed
items.summary: `score_of()` (`verifier.py:43-48`) runs a complete `scan_paths()` and keeps only the score, while `scan()` runs the same scan again for the diagnostics.
items.motivation: Measured on the vulnerable fixture: one run with one accepted patch made 4 full scanner invocations (2 scan, 2 score_of) for 12 findings. The scanner is the deterministic cost floor of every run and the only part of the pipeline whose speed we control - model latency is the provider's. Consolidating to one scan returning both diagnostics and summary is the cheapest real speedup available, and it is a precondition for any incremental or cached scan later.
acceptance_criteria: One scan per file state returns both diagnostics and score; `score_of` is removed or delegates to it
A counter-based test asserts the number of scanner invocations for a one-patch run does not exceed 2
The published scores and grades are unchanged for all three fixtures

items.title: docs: the curator's shipped comment points at a CHANGELOG.md that does not exist
items.summary: `sync_roadmap_issues.py:226` closes a shipped item with 'see the CHANGELOG entry for {version}'. There is no CHANGELOG.md anywhere in the repository.
items.motivation: Every issue this project closes as delivered ends with a dead instruction, in text posted by automation. For a project whose argument is that its claims are checkable, an automated comment pointing at a file that does not exist is a small but self-inflicted contradiction. It is also a prerequisite for the first tagged release (G8b): a release needs release notes.
acceptance_criteria: A `CHANGELOG.md` exists in Keep-a-Changelog form with an Unreleased section
The shipped comment either links a real section or stops mentioning the CHANGELOG
A test asserts any document path named in bot-generated text exists in the tree

items.title: chore(package): ship py.typed, add --version, and declare project URLs
items.summary: The package is typed under `mypy --strict` but ships no `py.typed`, has no `--version` flag (`vexar-autofix --version` is an argparse error), and `pyproject.toml` has no `[project.urls]`.
items.motivation: A downstream user importing `vexar_autofix` gets no type information despite the strict typing this repo enforces on itself, because `py.typed` is absent. `--version` is the first command anyone types against an installed CLI, and today it fails. `[project.urls]` is what puts Homepage and Issues links on the PyPI page that G8b will create. All three are one file and one flag; together they are the difference between 'installable' and 'published'.
acceptance_criteria: `py.typed` ships inside the wheel and `import vexar_autofix` is typed for a downstream mypy run
`vexar-autofix --version` and `vexar_autofix.__version__` agree with `pyproject.toml`
`[project.urls]` declares Homepage, Issues and Changelog
A test asserts the three version sources agree (the release workflow already checks two of them)

items.title: ci: the package claims to be OS Independent but CI only ever runs on Ubuntu
items.summary: `pyproject.toml` classifies `Operating System :: OS Independent` and the quickstart gives Windows PowerShell activation steps, but `.github/workflows/ci.yml:14` runs only `ubuntu-latest`.
items.motivation: The repository's own standard is that a claim should be checkable. Two platform claims are untested: the classifier, and the Windows instructions in the README that a new user will follow first. Nothing in the suite is obviously Linux-specific, which is exactly why a cheap matrix would settle it - and if something is path- or shell-sensitive, better to learn it in CI than in the first Windows bug report.
acceptance_criteria: The test job runs on `windows-latest` as well as `ubuntu-latest` (at least on one Python version)
The mock eval and the CLI smoke test run on both
If any test is genuinely platform-specific it is marked and the classifier is corrected rather than the test deleted

items.title: fix(demo): throttle the hosted demo endpoint - it spends provider money per request
items.summary: `demo/app.py` restricts input to the three bundled fixtures (good) but has no rate limit, no concurrency cap and no per-request budget, so a public endpoint with an API key behind it can be looped.
items.motivation: The Dockerfile commit reasoned that restricting fixtures 'keeps each run at a known handful of cheap model calls while making abuse pointless'. Known size is not the same as bounded spend: a loop still costs money and blocks the single worker, and the demo is the first thing a judge or a visitor touches. The fix is a token bucket plus a concurrency gate, which is a few lines.
acceptance_criteria: A per-IP rate limit and a global concurrency cap exist, both configurable by environment variable
Exceeding either returns a clear 429 with a Retry-After header, not a hang or a 500
A test drives the endpoint past the limit and asserts the provider client is not called again
The README states the demo's cost envelope

items.title: feat(agent): give every refusal a stable reason code
items.summary: The `refused` bucket carries prose in `why` and nothing a CI job can route on.
items.motivation: A machine consumer needs to distinguish 'this rule has no mechanical remedy, stop asking' from 'the model produced nothing usable, retry'. Prose answers neither. The codes are also the vocabulary the proof artifact will publish, so they have to exist before the artifact does.
acceptance_criteria: Every bucket entry carries a code from a closed enum: no_remedy, not_confirmed, unsafe_rule, ambiguous_anchor, verification_failed, tests_failed, model_no_edits
`why` is kept as the human string and never replaced by the code
--json exposes the code on every entry
A test asserts no bucket entry can exist without a code

items.title: feat(proof): emit a signed proof artifact for every run
items.summary: Evidence today is a terminal diff plus --json. A buyer wants a file they can attach to a ticket.
items.motivation: This is the moat made portable. A proof artifact is what turns 'trust us, we verified it' into an artifact a security team can file, diff between releases, and keep after the tool is uninstalled.
acceptance_criteria: --report PATH writes a versioned JSON document
It records target hash before/after, scanner and model versions, per-finding decision with code, the diff and the gate results
`verified` is true only when every gate passed
The file validates against docs/proof-artifact.schema.json
Output is deterministic apart from timestamps, pinned by a golden test

items.title: feat(cli): fix-policy flags so a team can bound what will be touched
items.summary: The set of fixable rules is global. A team cannot say 'fix timeouts only' or 'never touch this rule'.
items.motivation: Adoption stalls on the first reviewer who asks 'what stops this from rewriting the function I care about'. A bounded policy is the answer, and it costs almost nothing because the rule set is already a closed frozenset.
acceptance_criteria: --allow-rules, --block-rules and --require-approval RULES are implemented
A --policy preset exists: conservative (MCP010 only), default (all four), strict (approval for any patch that deletes a sink)
A blocked rule is reported, never attempted
An approval-required patch stops before writing and prints the exact command to apply it

items.title: feat(action): GitHub Action with preview, gate and apply modes
items.summary: There is no way to use this from CI without a local install and a key in the job.
items.motivation: The scanner already has an Action, so the child product has no entry point in the place where its parent is already used. Preview mode is the important one: it shows the diff on the PR and writes nothing, which is how a security team decides to trust the tool with apply mode.
acceptance_criteria: Three modes: preview (PR comment, never writes), gate (fail if a confirmed finding remains fixable), apply (commit to a branch)
Usable from a workflow file with no local install
A preview run on this repo's own fixtures is linked from the README

items.title: test(verifier): a rejection corpus of patches that must never be accepted
items.summary: The differentiator is refusing bad patches, and there is no public evidence of how often it refuses them.
items.motivation: A tool that says 'we catch bad fixes' is a claim. A corpus of named bad fixes, each with the verdict it must receive, is evidence. It also grows by itself: every real failure found becomes a case, so the number in the README only ever goes up.
acceptance_criteria: benchmarks/rejections/ holds every patch the audit must reject, with rule, reason and expected verdict
The accepted canonical set sits beside it so both sides are measured
The corpus runs in CI
The rejection count is published in the README and on the demo page and only grows

items.title: docs(proof): VERIFICATION.md - the command that reproduces every published number
items.summary: The README and demo page quote scores, finding counts and costs. The recipe to reproduce them is scattered across commits. (The telemetry half of the original G7 moved to N3, which fixes the numbers themselves.)
items.motivation: Every figure this project publishes is supposed to carry a timestamp and a commit. That only holds if a stranger can rerun the command and get the same number. Without this page, the honesty claim is a style of writing rather than a property of the repo.
acceptance_criteria: Every published number is listed with the exact command that produces it
Each entry names the commit and date it was captured at
Anything that cannot be reproduced offline says so explicitly
A stranger can re-derive the scanner half from a fresh clone without an API key

items.title: chore(release): rename the import package to vexar_mcp and publish to PyPI
items.summary: The distribution is Vexar-MCP but the import package is mcp_doctor, and that name belongs to a different project on PyPI.
items.motivation: Nothing can be published until this lands, and the pin in this repo points at a commit rather than a version because of it. The rename has to happen in the parent first, with a shim, then the two import sites here, then the release - in that order, in one coordinated change.
acceptance_criteria: Parent renames src/mcp_doctor to src/vexar_mcp and keeps an mcp_doctor shim for one minor version
This repo's imports move to vexar_mcp
The dependency pin moves from a commit SHA to a published version
`pip install vexar-mcp` and `pip install vexar-autofix` coexist with no file overlap

items.title: feat(cli): emit SARIF 2.1.0 verification report summarizing fixed vs refused findings per file
items.summary: CI security tabs consume SARIF, and multi-finding files need clear distinction between findings fixed+verified vs findings refused for human review.
items.motivation: Teams wiring `vexar-autofix` into GitHub Code Scanning need machine-readable SARIF results carrying the verifier verdict on each finding without losing line-level precision.
acceptance_criteria: `--sarif PATH` writes valid SARIF 2.1.0 output grouping multiple findings per file cleanly
Each SARIF result properties bag records the bucket (`fixed`, `human`, `refused`) and verifier status
Deterministic output covered by regression tests on `examples/vulnerable_server.py`
